title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows an AI coding and agent tool being used outside the conditions it was designed for. Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, was directed by Aurora ransomware operators to perform offensive security tasks: network scanning, privilege enumeration, and credential attacks against target organizations. The tool was not compromised or malfunctioning in a technical sense, it was being operated as intended, but by actors using it for purposes its deployment context does not authorize.

The failure mode is misuse rather than model error. The system executed the tasks it was given, which means the gap was not in model behavior but in access controls and use-policy enforcement upstream of the model. Catching this would have required either restrictions on the categories of commands the agent would accept, behavioral monitoring for sequences consistent with offensive operations, or identity and intent verification at onboarding, none of which are inherent to the tool as described.

What is not established is the full extent of harm: the reporting identifies ten organizations targeted in one cluster and eight in another, but the number successfully compromised and the scale of any data loss or encryption are not confirmed by the sources summarized here. An allegation of involvement by Russian-speaking cybercriminals is present in the reporting but is not a legal finding.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Security researchers at Gambit Security discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been actively targeting ESXi servers since April 2026. The group developed a Linux variant of their ransomware that can encrypt virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. Researchers also found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks across ten organizations between April and May 2026. The agent was tasked with various hacking activities including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and credential attacks, though many attempts failed initially.

Additionally, researchers identified a second cluster of Aurora activity affecting eight organizations across multiple countries. This second group used different tactics, including SQL Server exploitation and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. The investigation revealed multiple command and control servers, SOCKS proxies, and the group's data leak website at exposedrecords.io. Researchers published technical indicators including IP addresses, file hashes, and domains associated with both Aurora clusters to help organizations identify and defend against these attacks.
